Excuse me, is this the line for registration? Oh good, thank you. I'm Emre, from Ankara. I'm a neurologist, but I also do some research on pain. I saw on your badge that you're from Brazil. That's a long trip! I came yesterday, and I still don't know where anything is. Do you know where the workshop on nerve damage is going to be? I think it starts at eleven.

Thank you, Dejair. We have a few minutes for questions, so let me start with one from the audience and one of my own. The first is about your method. You measured pain with a questionnaire, but some of your patients cannot read very well. So how did you make sure the answers were reliable? Did somebody read the questions to them? And my own question is about time. You followed the patients for six months. Do you think the effect lasts longer than that, or do you expect it to go down? If you don't have data on that yet, that is fine, just tell us what you expect. We have about three minutes, so please keep it short.

Very nice poster. But can I ask you about this number here? You say seventy percent of patients felt less pain after the treatment. Seventy percent is a lot. In our study in Moscow, with a similar drug, we saw something like forty percent. So I am a little surprised. How did you measure less pain? Was it the patient who said it, or was it a doctor? Because patients often feel better when they know they are receiving a new treatment. And another thing: you had no control group, right? So how can you back up this number? I am not saying it is wrong. Maybe your patients are different from ours. Maybe the dose is different. But I think you need to explain this difference, because many people at this congress will ask you the same question.

Sorry, could you tell me what you mean by reliable? So you're asking if the answers were correct, is that right? I'm not one hundred percent sure, but I think they were. That's because a nurse read every question to the patients. If you're interested, I'll send you the protocol.
